articles.title: When Certainty Becomes Good News: Markets After the 2026 Midterms
articles.dek: Stocks soared and oil sank after the US midterms. What does a market's mood really tell us?
paras: On the morning of November 4, 2026, investors around the world woke up to the results of the United States midterm elections, in which the Democratic Party won control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate. What happened next surprised many casual observers. Overnight, futures contracts linked to the technology-heavy Nasdaq index had fallen by as much as 2.5 percent as the results emerged, yet by the end of the trading day the Dow Jones Industrial Average had climbed roughly 3 percent, its strongest single-day performance in well over a year, while the broader S&P 500 rose about 1.6 percent. At the same time, the price of crude oil collapsed by around 8 percent, and gold jumped back above 4,000 dollars an ounce. To understand why markets reacted this way, it helps to look beyond which party won and to consider how financial markets process information.

A central idea in finance is that markets dislike uncertainty more than they dislike bad news. Share prices reflect investors' collective expectations about companies' future profits, and those expectations depend partly on government policy—taxes, regulation, trade rules, and public spending. Before an election, traders must assign probabilities to several possible futures at once, and many respond by holding back or demanding a higher return for the risk they bear. Once the outcome is known, that hedging can unwind quickly. As one strategist at the brokerage Charles Schwab put it, markets typically respond positively to midterm elections being over, “no matter what the outcome.” In other words, part of the rally may have been a release of tension rather than a verdict on any party's program.

A second explanation concerns the structure of government. Because the president belongs to a different party from the new congressional majority, many analysts expect a period of “gridlock,” in which few major laws pass. For investors, gridlock can paradoxically be attractive. It reduces the likelihood of sweeping changes to taxation or regulation, and it may restrain large increases in government borrowing, which in turn can help keep interest rates in check. Bond markets appeared to share this view: the yield on ten-year US Treasury bonds slipped to around 4.9 percent.

The oil market told a different but related story. Energy prices had surged earlier in the year after the outbreak of conflict involving Iran, pushing up the cost of fuel and shipping worldwide. Reuters reported that the fall in oil prices on November 4 was linked to rising hopes that the conflict could be brought to an end through diplomacy, with Qatar stepping up its mediation efforts. Cheaper oil tends to ease inflation, because energy feeds into the price of almost everything that must be manufactured or transported. Lower expected inflation, in turn, makes both stocks and bonds more appealing.

Not every corner of the market celebrated, however. Energy companies, whose revenues depend directly on the price of crude, fell by nearly 5 percent as a group. Shares of several chipmakers and data-center suppliers also declined, as some investors worried that a Democratic Congress might scrutinize the rapid expansion of artificial-intelligence infrastructure more closely. Meanwhile, sectors such as health care and consumer goods posted strong gains. Such divergence is a reminder that “the market” is not a single entity with a single opinion but an aggregate of millions of decisions, each reflecting a particular bet about who will win and who will lose under new conditions.

Some economists caution against reading too much into a single day of trading. Short-term price swings are often driven by algorithmic trading and by investors adjusting positions they had taken before the vote, and such moves can reverse within weeks. Moreover, the long-run performance of stock markets has historically depended far more on corporate earnings, productivity, and interest rates than on which party controls Congress. From this perspective, the dramatic headlines of November 4 reveal more about investor psychology than about the economy's true direction.

Others argue that markets, however noisy, contain useful information precisely because participants risk their own money. If the price of oil drops sharply, for example, traders are signaling that they now see a meaningful chance of lower energy costs ahead, a forecast that affects households, airlines, and governments alike. The challenge for observers, then, is to treat market reactions neither as infallible predictions nor as meaningless noise, but as one source of evidence to be weighed against others.

articles.title: Who Is Responsible When Software Acts on Its Own? Apple's Warning About AI Agents
articles.dek: Apple has formally warned that AI agents may act in unpredictable ways. Who is responsible when they do?
paras: Every year, large American companies must file a detailed annual report, known as a Form 10-K, with the US Securities and Exchange Commission. Among its many sections is a list of “risk factors”—developments that could harm the company's business and, therefore, its investors. These lists are usually dry and predictable, but in early November 2026 one item in Apple's filing attracted widespread attention. In what news outlets described as one of the first cases of its kind, a major technology company formally warned investors that artificial-intelligence “agents” could behave in ways that are “unintended or unpredictable.”

To understand why this matters, it is important to distinguish AI agents from the chatbots that became popular earlier in the decade. A chatbot answers questions; a person reads the answer and decides what to do with it. An agent, by contrast, is designed to take actions on a user's behalf: booking a flight, sending an email, moving money between accounts, or adjusting the settings of a smart home. The appeal is obvious. Instead of switching between a dozen apps, a user could simply state a goal and let the software work out the steps. Technology companies have invested heavily in this vision, and Apple itself has recently begun allowing outside developers to connect their apps' content and functions to its Siri assistant.

Yet the same autonomy that makes agents useful also makes them risky. According to reports on the filing, Apple cautioned that agents might exceed the permissions they have been given, fail to follow instructions, or take actions that are difficult to reverse. The last concern is especially significant, because while a faulty answer from a chatbot can simply be ignored, an agent that has already transferred funds, deleted files, or shared private data with the wrong recipient may have caused harm that no software update can undo. Apple also noted that such failures could expose it to lawsuits and damage its reputation.

Behind these warnings lies a difficult legal question: when an agent makes a costly mistake, who is responsible? Possible candidates include the user who gave the instruction, the company that designed the device, the developer of the app the agent used, and the firm that built the underlying AI model. Existing product-liability laws were written for tools that do what they are told, and they fit uneasily with systems that interpret goals and choose their own methods. Some legal scholars argue that new rules will be needed, perhaps requiring companies to keep detailed records of every action an agent takes so that errors can be traced.

Not everyone sees the filing as a sign of alarm. Risk-factor sections are, in part, a legal shield: by disclosing possible dangers in advance, companies reduce the chance that investors can later claim they were misled. Seen this way, Apple's warning may say more about cautious lawyers than about any specific failure. Indeed, the filing reportedly did not describe any particular incident that prompted the new language. Supporters of rapid development also point out that every powerful technology, from automobiles to the internet, carried risks that society learned to manage through experience rather than by waiting for perfect safety.

Critics respond that agents differ from earlier technologies in one crucial way: they make decisions at a speed and scale that humans cannot easily monitor. A single flawed instruction, copied across millions of devices, could produce millions of errors before anyone notices. For this reason, a growing number of companies are developing safeguards. The cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike, for instance, has introduced what it calls an “AI kill switch,” allowing administrators to halt an agent that behaves abnormally, and some websites have begun blocking automated agents from accessing their services altogether.

The most balanced position may be that Apple's disclosure is both routine and revealing. It is routine because companies are expected to list foreseeable risks; it is revealing because AI agents have now moved from science fiction into the category of foreseeable risks at all. Whether these systems ultimately earn public trust may depend less on how intelligent they become than on whether users can understand, limit, and, when necessary, stop what they do.

articles.title: Messages in a Grain of Dust: Life's Building Blocks on Asteroid Ryugu
articles.dek: Tiny grains from asteroid Ryugu contain all five “letters” of life's genetic code. Here is what that does, and does not, prove.
paras: In December 2020, a small capsule parachuted into the Australian outback carrying a few grams of dark, crumbly material. It had been collected from Ryugu, a carbon-rich asteroid roughly 900 meters across, by the Japanese spacecraft Hayabusa2. Since then, scientists around the world have studied these grains in search of clues about the early solar system. In 2026, a team led by Toshiki Koga of the Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology reported in the journal Nature Astronomy that two Ryugu samples contain all five nucleobases used by living things—adenine, guanine, cytosine, thymine, and uracil. The finding, widely discussed again in recent weeks, adds weight to a long-standing idea: that some of the raw ingredients for life on Earth may have been delivered from space.

Nucleobases are the “letters” of the genetic code. In DNA, adenine, guanine, cytosine, and thymine pair up to store hereditary information; in RNA, uracil takes the place of thymine. Chemists divide these molecules into two families: purines (adenine and guanine), which have a double-ring structure, and pyrimidines (cytosine, thymine, and uracil), which have a single ring. Because these compounds are central to biology, finding them beyond Earth raises an obvious question: could they form through ordinary chemistry, without any living organism involved?

Earlier evidence came mainly from meteorites—fragments of asteroids that fall to Earth. Analyses of the famous Murchison meteorite, which landed in Australia in 1969, detected several nucleobases. However, such findings have always faced a serious objection. A meteorite that plunges through the atmosphere and sits on the ground, sometimes for years, is exposed to Earth's microbes, water, and soil. Critics could therefore argue that any biological molecules discovered inside it might simply be contamination from our own planet rather than evidence of chemistry in space.

This is where sample-return missions become valuable. The Ryugu grains were gathered directly from the asteroid, sealed in a capsule, and handled in carefully controlled clean facilities. To strengthen their case further, Koga's team ran identical tests on “blank” materials, such as sea sand and the mineral serpentine, to make sure that the nucleobases were not being introduced by the laboratory itself. NASA's OSIRIS-REx mission, which returned samples from the asteroid Bennu, had produced a similar result in 2025, so two independent missions now point in the same direction.

The details also reveal something interesting. In the Ryugu samples, purines and pyrimidines appeared in roughly equal amounts. In contrast, Murchison is richer in purines, while Bennu and another meteorite, Orgueil, contain more pyrimidines. The researchers suggest that these differences reflect the distinct chemical histories of each parent body; reports on the study note that the balance between the two families appears to vary with the amount of ammonia present. If so, nucleobases may form through several chemical pathways, which would make them more common across the solar system than once assumed.

Still, scientists urge caution about what the discovery does and does not show. The nucleobases occur only in trace amounts, far smaller than those of amino acids, another class of organic molecules found in asteroids. More fundamentally, possessing the letters of a language is not the same as writing a book. Life requires these molecules to link into long chains, to copy themselves, and to be enclosed within cell-like structures—steps that no asteroid sample has demonstrated. Some researchers also point out that nucleobases could have formed on the early Earth itself, for instance near volcanic vents or in shallow pools, making delivery from space unnecessary.

The likeliest answer may combine both views. Early Earth was bombarded by asteroids and comets for hundreds of millions of years, and each impact could have added organic material to whatever chemistry was already occurring locally. Seen this way, Ryugu does not solve the mystery of life's origin, but it narrows the range of possibilities. It shows that the ingredients for genetics were not unique to our planet and may have been scattered widely across the young solar system—waiting, in some places at least, for the right conditions to come together.

keySentences.text: adds weight to a long-standing idea: that some of the raw ingredients for life on Earth may have been delivered from space.
keySentences.note: Notice “some” and “may have been”. The discovery supports an idea; it does not prove it.

keySentences.text: However, such findings have always faced a serious objection.
keySentences.note: “However” introduces the problem with meteorite evidence: contamination. Paragraph 4 then answers it.

keySentences.text: This is where sample-return missions become valuable.
keySentences.note: Problem → solution. The paragraph lists three things that make the Ryugu results reliable, which a NOT question tests.

keySentences.text: If so, nucleobases may form through several chemical pathways, which would make them more common across the solar system than once assumed.
keySentences.note: A conditional chain (“If so … would”). Inference questions often ask what follows from it.

keySentences.text: More fundamentally, possessing the letters of a language is not the same as writing a book.
keySentences.note: An analogy: having the building blocks of life is not the same as life itself.

keySentences.text: Seen this way, Ryugu does not solve the mystery of life's origin, but it narrows the range of possibilities.
keySentences.note: The author's balanced conclusion: progress, not a final answer.

write.p: Professor: Scientists recently confirmed that samples from the asteroid Ryugu contain all five building blocks of DNA and RNA. Missions like this are extremely expensive. Some people believe governments should keep funding space exploration because it expands human knowledge. Others think the money would be better spent on urgent problems on Earth. Which position do you support, and why? (Aisha says space research pays off in unexpected ways. Daniel says priorities matter when people lack clean water and hospitals.)
